latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Bacteria from an intra-abdominal focus such as appendicitis, diverticulitis, colorectal malignancy, bowel perforation, or pylephlebitis reach hepatic sinusoids via the portal venous system and seed liver parenchyma.
Ascending infection from cholangitis, obstructed bile ducts, hepatolithiasis, biliary stents, or biliary-enteric communication seeds periportal liver and sustains enteric bacterial growth.
Sustained bacteremia from endocarditis, catheter infection, skin/soft tissue infection, or another distant focus seeds hepatic arterial inflow and produces single or multiple hepatic abscesses.
Kupffer-cell overflow and neutrophil recruitment form suppurative foci in hepatic parenchyma, producing fever, right upper quadrant pain, acute-phase reactants, and liver enzyme abnormalities.

Coalescence of suppurative foci into an encapsulated pus cavity with liquefaction, septations, poor antibiotic penetration, and need for image-guided or surgical drainage when large, multiloculated, ruptured, or clinically nonresponsive.

Enterobacterales, streptococci, enterococci, and anaerobes may coexist in a low-oxygen pus cavity; anaerobes are often culture-negative and require empiric coverage when bowel or biliary source is plausible.

Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae, classically associated with diabetes and K1/K2-like virulence programs, can cause cryptogenic liver abscess with bacteremia and metastatic infection including endogenous endophthalmitis or CNS infection.
PAMP-driven IL-1, IL-6, TNF, and acute-phase response from hepatic and circulating innate immune cells, driving fever, rigors, leukocytosis, CRP/procalcitonin rise, tachycardia, and malaise.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Septic organ dysfunction from liver abscess
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Bacteremia, cytokine surge, vasoplegia, hypoperfusion, and coagulopathy produce hypotension, lactate elevation, AKI, encephalopathy, DIC, ARDS, and high short-term mortality risk.
Large, multiloculated, viscous, inaccessible, ruptured, or incompletely drained abscess cavities continue to sustain bacterial burden despite active antibiotics.
High-pressure or superficially located abscess erodes into peritoneum, pleura, pericardium, diaphragm, or adjacent viscera, causing peritonitis, empyema, fistula, or sudden shock physiology.
Suppurative thrombophlebitis in the portal venous system can be a source or complication of liver abscess, sustaining fever, bacteremia, liver seeding, and portal/hepatic perfusion injury.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Portal pyemia delivers organisms to hepatic sinusoids, overwhelming local phagocytic clearance and initiating suppuration.
Infected obstructed bile or segmental cholangitis seeds periportal hepatic tissue.
Persistent bacteremia can seed liver through hepatic arterial flow, especially with staphylococcal or streptococcal sources.
Neutrophilic foci liquefy and coalesce into a drainable pus cavity.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Risk amplified by large diameter, multiloculation, thick pus, deep inaccessible location, or delayed drainage.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Mature pus cavities are poorly sterilized by antibiotics alone and can remain an active focus until drained.
Mixed aerobic and anaerobic flora thrive in low-oxygen pus and sustain cavity formation.
Undrained pus maintains bacterial biomass despite active serum antibiotic concentrations.
Ongoing bacterial shedding and antigen release from an undrained abscess sustains fever and acute-phase response.
Bacterial PAMP exposure drives IL-1, IL-6, TNF, CRP, and procalcitonin response.
Hypervirulent Klebsiella often produces bacteremia and intense systemic inflammation even without biliary disease.
Sustained cytokine signaling causes vasoplegia, endothelial activation, capillary leak, and hypoperfusion.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Risk rises with large, superficial, left-lobe/subcapsular, gas-forming, or delayed-drainage abscesses.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Expanding pus cavity can erode through capsule or diaphragm.
Intra-abdominal suppurative processes can infect portal venous thrombus while seeding the liver.
Suppurative portal thrombosis can continuously shed organisms into the liver and form additional abscess foci.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Fever may be blunted in elderly, cirrhotic, uremic, or steroid-treated patients.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: IL-1, IL-6, TNF, and prostaglandin signaling reset hypothalamic set-point.
Bacteremic showers from abscess commonly produce chills and rigors.
Fever, pain, hypovolemia, and catecholamine response drive tachycardia.
Fever, cytokine-driven respiratory drive, and metabolic acidosis increase respiratory rate.
Septic vasodilation and capillary leak lower MAP.
Septic shock physiology reduces systolic pressure.
Hypoperfusion, adrenergic stress, and impaired oxygen utilization increase lactate.
Septic hypoperfusion and nephrotoxic exposures can produce AKI.
Renal hypoperfusion and AKI reduce urine output.
Septic encephalopathy, hypoperfusion, fever, and metabolic derangements can cause delirium or altered mentation.
Sepsis-associated platelet consumption and DIC physiology lower platelets.
DIC, hepatic dysfunction, vitamin K deficiency, or cholestasis can prolong INR.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Leukopenia can occur in severe sepsis, marrow suppression, or advanced cirrhosis.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Acute bacterial inflammation mobilizes neutrophils.
Neutrophilic predominance is typical in pyogenic abscess.
IL-6 drives hepatic CRP production with a 24-48 hour lag.
Bacterial systemic inflammation and bacteremia raise procalcitonin.
Capsular stretch and adjacent peritoneal inflammation produce right upper quadrant pain.
Diaphragmatic irritation can refer pain to the right shoulder via the phrenic nerve.
Hepatic inflammation and mass effect can enlarge or tender the liver.
Periportal inflammation and biliary compression commonly elevate ALP.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Stronger when biliary obstruction, cholangitis, or multiple abscesses are present.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Inflammatory cholestasis or biliary obstruction raises bilirubin.
Local hepatocyte stress and inflammation produce mild to moderate ALT elevation.
Local hepatocyte stress and sepsis-related hepatic injury elevate AST.
Inflammation, capillary leak, malnutrition, and hepatic dysfunction lower albumin.
A mature abscess cavity is the imaging finding defining the disease manifold.
Cavity maturation and ongoing pus production enlarge the abscess.
Portal pyemia and pylephlebitis can seed multiple hepatic foci rather than a solitary abscess.
Complex pus and partially separated foci produce septated or multiloculated imaging pattern.
Gas-forming organisms or communication with bowel/biliary tract can produce gas in the abscess cavity.
Capsular breach produces imaging or operative evidence of rupture.
Subdiaphragmatic inflammation can cause reactive right pleural effusion or empyema.
Suppurative portal thrombosis is detected as portal/mesenteric venous thrombus with infectious context on CT or Doppler imaging.
Biliary-origin abscess often coexists with stone, stricture, stent occlusion, or malignant obstruction.
Cholangitis, jaundice, biliary dilation, or recent biliary instrumentation support biliary source.
Diverticulitis, appendicitis, colorectal malignancy, perforation, or inflammatory bowel disease raises intra-abdominal source probability.
A mature collection visible on US/CT/MRI creates a drainable focus.
Persistent infection in a drainable pus cavity creates procedural source-control need.
Ongoing fever or cavity persistence after drainage indicates inadequate source control.
Persistent fever, leukocytosis, or pain after active therapy suggests drainage failure, resistant pathogen, or missed source.
Aspirated pus often yields causative bacteria, though prior antibiotics and anaerobic handling reduce yield.
Bacterial burden in pus drives Gram stain/culture positivity.
Bacteremia is common in pyogenic liver abscess, especially Klebsiella or biliary-source disease.
The hypervirulent phenotype is represented by high probability of Klebsiella pneumoniae as the abscess organism.
Hypervirulent Klebsiella liver abscess can metastatically seed the eye.
Metastatic CNS infection including meningitis or brain abscess is a recognized invasive Klebsiella complication.
Subcapsular or large abscesses can rupture into peritoneal or pleural spaces.
Active portal venous septic thrombosis increases hazard of persistent pylephlebitis and further seeding.
Vasoplegia and hypoperfusion can progress to septic shock.
Hypoperfusion, inflammation, contrast, and antibiotics raise AKI risk.
Sepsis-induced coagulopathy can evolve into DIC.
Severe sepsis and metastatic pulmonary involvement can trigger ARDS.
Residual cavity, persistent biliary pathology, or unresolved bowel source increases recurrence.
Rupture with peritonitis/empyema sharply worsens short-term survival.
Shock, AKI, respiratory failure, DIC, and ICU-level illness dominate near-term mortality.
Undrained or incompletely drained infection sustains sepsis and recurrence risk.
Added during horizontal ontology audit: this axis is a real shared inflammatory/CNS involvement feature for this disease family, not a case-specific ranking patch.
Severe systemic infection, shock, hypoxemia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, or fluid overload can increase oxygen or ventilatory support needs; this parallels the existing ards_hazard pathway.

Shaking chills/rigors during bacteremic fever spikes.
Sinus tachycardia tracking fever, pain, dehydration, and sepsis.
Tachypnea from fever, pain, sepsis, pleural irritation, or metabolic acidosis.

Usually normal unless pleural/pulmonary extension, ARDS, pneumonia, or fluid overload occurs.

Subacute anorexia and inflammation can cause weight loss.

Probability that portal seeding from appendicitis, diverticulitis, colorectal malignancy, perforation, or other bowel source is present.
Probability that imaging shows a drainable hepatic collection.
Need for abscess drainage, biliary decompression, surgery, or source correction.
Adequacy of abscess drainage and correction of biliary/intra-abdominal source.
Persistent fever, pain, leukocytosis, CRP/procalcitonin elevation, or enlarging cavity after active antibiotics.
Probability of pathogen recovery from blood culture before antibiotics.
Approximate bloodstream bacterial burden; often low but clinically decisive when positive.
Probability that aspirated pus yields a pathogen; reduced by prior antibiotics or poor anaerobic handling.
Pathogen load in abscess aspirate; used as a microbiology context rather than routine presentation evidence.
Probability that bloodstream pathogen is gram-negative Enterobacterales or another gram-negative organism.
Probability that anaerobic bacteria materially contribute to the abscess, especially bowel/biliary source or polymicrobial infection.
Probability that Klebsiella pneumoniae is the causative organism; context includes diabetes, cryptogenic abscess, East/Southeast Asian epidemiology, and metastatic infection.
Probability that the administered regimen covers the causative organism(s) at the abscess site.
Probability that Enterobacterales isolate is ceftriaxone-susceptible.

Probability that isolate is susceptible to ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin; important for oral step-down.
Risk of ESBL-producing Enterobacterales based on prior colonization, recent antibiotics, healthcare exposure, or local ecology.

Hazard of clinically important bleeding from coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, anticoagulation, or procedures.
Hazard of C. difficile, fungal, resistant bacterial, or nosocomial secondary infection during prolonged broad-spectrum therapy or immune dysfunction.
Hazard of progression to vasopressor-requiring septic shock.
Hazard of AKI from sepsis, hypoperfusion, contrast, aminoglycosides, or baseline CKD.
Hazard of overt DIC in severe sepsis or shock.
Hazard of ARDS from severe sepsis, pulmonary metastatic infection, or pleural extension.
Hazard of rupture into peritoneal, pleural, pericardial, or adjacent visceral space.
Hazard of suppurative portal or mesenteric venous thrombosis.
Hazard of metastatic endogenous endophthalmitis, especially with hypervirulent Klebsiella bacteremia.
Hazard of metastatic CNS infection such as meningitis or brain abscess.
Bleeding hazard from percutaneous transhepatic drainage or surgery, modulated by INR, platelets, anticoagulation, and vascular anatomy.
Hazard of recurrent liver abscess after apparent clinical resolution, higher with persistent biliary tract disease or incomplete source correction.
Lifespan outcome hazard emerging from septic shock, rupture, organ failure, malignancy/cirrhosis/CKD context, delayed antibiotics, and source-control failure.
Nonspecific systemic inflammatory marker that commonly rises in clinically significant pulmonary, metastatic, or disseminated infection; included through horizontal fairness audit.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Effective drainage plus active antibiotics usually produces defervescence over 48-72 hours.
CRP falls after adequate source control with a slower lag than fever.
Large abscesses are less likely to sterilize with antibiotics alone and more likely to need drainage.
Multiloculation makes needle aspiration and single-catheter drainage less complete.
Biliary obstruction creates conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in biliary-origin abscess.
When bilirubin rises from cholestasis, the direct fraction dominates.
Transaminases co-rise with hepatic inflammation or shock liver.
Shock and vasopressor-requiring hypoperfusion strongly increase AKI hazard.
DIC or sepsis coagulopathy raises bleeding risk during transhepatic drainage or surgery.
Rupture causing peritonitis, empyema, or shock materially raises death hazard.
Septic shock is the dominant near-term mortality driver.
Both metastatic hazards share hypervirulent Klebsiella bacteremia as an upstream driver rather than one directly causing the other.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ceftriaxone activity against susceptible Enterobacterales and streptococci is needed for the aerobic component.
ESBL organisms are not reliably covered by ceftriaxone.
Metronidazole covers anaerobes that are common in bowel/biliary-source abscess and hard to culture.
Severe cephalosporin/beta-lactam reaction precludes routine use.
Antibiotics alone may fail when a mature large or multiloculated pus cavity is present.

failure_modes: Uncorrected biliary obstruction or bowel source

side_effects.interpretation: Ceftriaxone can rarely cause biliary sludge or cholestatic lab noise.
Prolonged broad antibiotic exposure increases C. difficile and secondary infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Common broad regimen when ceftriaxone-susceptible Enterobacterales or streptococci plus anaerobic coverage are plausible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Susceptibility delivers aerobic gram-negative coverage with anaerobic and many enterococcal effects.
High ESBL probability lowers reliability, especially with bacteremia or severe illness.
Antipseudomonal activity can matter after healthcare or biliary instrumentation.
Renal dose adjustment is required.
Severe immediate beta-lactam reaction precludes routine use.
Antibiotic effect is limited when a large pus cavity remains undrained.

side_effects.interpretation: AKI risk, especially with vancomycin or baseline renal impairment.
Broad-spectrum exposure selects resistant organisms and C. difficile.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad single-agent regimen for polymicrobial hepatic abscess when antipseudomonal and anaerobic coverage are needed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cefepime adds antipseudomonal activity; metronidazole supplies anaerobic abscess coverage.
Cefepime may be unreliable for ESBL high-inoculum abscess/bacteremia.
Renal adjustment is needed to reduce neurotoxicity risk.
Severe beta-lactam reaction precludes routine cefepime use.

side_effects.interpretation: Cefepime neurotoxicity risk rises with renal impairment.

treatments.context_specific_role: Antipseudomonal beta-lactam option paired with anaerobic coverage when cefepime susceptibility and renal dosing are acceptable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Carbapenems reliably cover ESBL Enterobacterales when susceptible.
Carbapenem-resistant organism requires alternate targeted therapy.
CRE risk reduces expected activity pending susceptibility.
Severe allergy requires specialist risk assessment or desensitization/alternate regimen.
Renal dosing reduces neurotoxicity and seizure risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Broad carbapenem exposure increases C. difficile and resistant organism selection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad regimen when ESBL risk, severe sepsis, healthcare exposure, or polymicrobial gram-negative abscess makes narrower beta-lactams unreliable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ertapenem covers susceptible ESBL Enterobacterales and anaerobes.
Ertapenem lacks Pseudomonas activity.
CRE risk undermines ertapenem.

side_effects.interpretation: Broad anaerobic and gram-negative exposure can select C. difficile or resistant organisms.

treatments.context_specific_role: Once-daily option for susceptible ESBL or polymicrobial abscess when Pseudomonas and Enterococcus coverage are not needed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Activity requires isolate susceptibility.
Oral step-down is more reliable after drainage and clinical improvement.
Drug interactions and liver disease can complicate safety monitoring.

failure_modes: No anaerobic coverage if metronidazole omitted
QT prolongation or tendon/CNS toxicity risk

side_effects.interpretation: Fluoroquinolones can cause CNS effects, especially in older adults or renal impairment.

treatments.context_specific_role: Culture-directed oral or IV option when susceptibility is known and source control is adequate, or as part of a beta-lactam-sparing regimen.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Staphylococcal bacteremia, endocarditis, catheter, or skin source raises gram-positive coverage need.
Vancomycin has no gram-negative activity.
AUC-guided monitoring and renal dosing are needed.

side_effects.interpretation: Nephrotoxicity risk, especially with piperacillin-tazobactam or baseline AKI.

treatments.context_specific_role: Add-on only when gram-positive bacteremia, catheter/endocarditis source, MRSA risk, or Enterococcus concern is plausible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Catheter drainage requires a safe drainable collection.
Larger abscesses are more likely to need continuous catheter drainage.
Multiloculation can require multiple catheters, repeated intervention, or surgery.
Coagulopathy must be corrected or route reconsidered.

side_effects.interpretation: Transhepatic drainage can cause bleeding, especially with coagulopathy.
Bile leak or biliary irritation can transiently worsen cholestatic labs.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source-control procedure for drainable pyogenic liver abscess, especially large, persistent, or septic presentations.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Needle aspiration is more feasible for smaller or simpler cavities and can provide culture.
Multiloculated abscess often needs catheter drainage or surgery instead of single aspiration.
Repeated aspiration or catheter conversion may be needed if fever persists.

treatments.context_specific_role: Diagnostic and partial source-control procedure for small or simple abscesses, or when culture is needed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rupture with peritonitis or uncontrolled contamination often needs operative source control.
Complex multiloculated abscess can fail percutaneous drainage.
Surgery is a rescue pathway after incomplete percutaneous drainage or uncorrected intra-abdominal pathology.
Operative risk rises in shock; benefit depends on whether surgery can control the source.

side_effects.interpretation: Perioperative risk rises in frail or shock patients; benefit depends on source control.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue or definitive source control for rupture, failed percutaneous drainage, multiloculated inaccessible collections, or concurrent surgical intra-abdominal pathology.

treatments.drug: ERCP or percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Biliary decompression directly treats obstructed infected bile when biliary source is active.
Benefit is largest when the abscess is driven by cholangitis, stent occlusion, stone, or stricture.
Drainage and sphincterotomy bleeding risk rises with coagulopathy.

failure_modes: Persistent hepatic cavity requiring separate abscess drainage

side_effects.interpretation: Sphincterotomy or transhepatic drainage can cause bleeding.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source-control pathway when biliary obstruction, cholangitis, or stent/stone/stricture contributes to the abscess.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluids improve effective circulating volume in septic hypoperfusion.
Volume overload risk requires dynamic reassessment.

side_effects.interpretation: Over-resuscitation can worsen oxygenation through pulmonary edema.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supportive hemodynamic stabilization for septic hypoperfusion while antibiotics and source control address the causal field.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vasopressor benefit exists when hypotension persists despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
Norepinephrine supports perfusion but does not sterilize or drain the abscess.

failure_modes: Arrhythmia or ischemia at high doses

side_effects.interpretation: High catecholamine exposure can contribute to lactate signal even as perfusion improves.

treatments.context_specific_role: Perfusion support for liver-abscess septic shock; outcome improvement depends on concurrent antibiotics and source control.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Anticoagulation is considered when septic portal venous thrombosis is documented, alongside antibiotics and source control.
Active bleeding, severe coagulopathy, or high-risk drainage route may preclude anticoagulation.

side_effects.interpretation: Bleeding hazard rises around drainage procedures or with coagulopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct for documented pylephlebitis; not a routine liver abscess treatment when portal thrombosis is absent.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises biliary seeding, polymicrobial infection, enterococcal/anaerobic involvement, recurrence, and need for biliary decompression.
Raises Klebsiella probability, gas-forming abscess risk, metastatic infection risk, and severity of sepsis.

over_65.trajectory_modulation: More biliary disease, malignancy, muted pain/fever, septic shock, ICU admission, and mortality.

present.trajectory_modulation: Epidemiologic enrichment without a distinct disease mechanism.
Raises portal venous seeding, polymicrobial/anaerobic abscess probability, multiple abscess count, and recurrence unless the bowel source is addressed.
Blunts fever and leukocytosis while increasing bacteremia, fungal/opportunistic infection, source-control failure, and mortality.
Raises mortality, coagulopathy, procedure bleeding risk, atypical fever, and hepatic decompensation.
Raises AKI consequences, antibiotic dosing complexity, and mortality; creatinine background should be CKD-adjusted.
Raises ESBL, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, and initial inactive therapy risk.
Raises cryptogenic Klebsiella abscess probability and metastatic eye/CNS infection hazards.
Raises drainage need, source-control failure, recurrence, and rupture hazard.
Sustains abscess burden and cytokine response; raises septic shock, rupture, recurrence, and mortality.

supportive_care: Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when this does not delay therapy; start broad active coverage promptly in septic or unstable patients.
Use contrast CT abdomen or high-quality ultrasound/MRI to define abscess size, number, location, gas, multiloculation, rupture, biliary obstruction, and drainable window.

Send aspirated pus for Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic cultures with susceptibility; consider fungal, mycobacterial, Entamoeba, or Echinococcus testing only when exposure or imaging context supports it.
Trend temperature, heart rate, MAP, urine output, WBC/ANC, platelets, CRP, procalcitonin, bilirubin, ALP, AST/ALT, creatinine, lactate, and INR to judge response.
Re-image or reassess drainage if fever, pain, leukocytosis, CRP/procalcitonin, or bacteremia persists after 48-72 hours of active antibiotics and attempted source control.

Coordinate interventional radiology, infectious diseases, hepatobiliary surgery, and gastroenterology early when the abscess is large, multiloculated, ruptured, left-lobe/subcapsular, biliary-associated, or clinically severe.
Correct coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia when feasible before transhepatic drainage or surgery; balance against delay when source control is urgent.
Adjust antibiotic dosing for renal and hepatic function; de-escalate to culture-directed therapy when susceptibilities and source control status are clear.
Maintain anaerobic coverage when bowel or biliary source is plausible because anaerobic cultures may be falsely negative.

Screen for metastatic infection symptoms in Klebsiella-associated or bacteremic disease, especially visual symptoms, headache, meningismus, focal neurologic deficits, pulmonary nodules, or skin/soft tissue lesions.
Evaluate for underlying biliary disease, colorectal malignancy, diverticulitis, appendicitis, endocarditis, catheter infection, or immunosuppression when the source is not obvious.

Use sepsis supportive care as needed: balanced crystalloid, lactate reassessment, norepinephrine for fluid-refractory hypotension, oxygen/ventilatory support, glycemic control, VTE prophylaxis when safe, and renal replacement therapy for standard indications.

Plan follow-up imaging because radiographic cavity resolution lags clinical improvement; avoid extending therapy solely for residual scar-like imaging if clinical and inflammatory markers have resolved.
Address recurrence prevention by correcting biliary obstruction/stents/stones or bowel source, and arranging follow-up for diabetes control, malignancy workup, and drain management.
